blocks.robotComment: Every tool in this whole track — Git, hosting, Expo, all of it — gets typed into this same window. 💻
blocks.body: A terminal (also called a command line, console, or shell) is a text-based way to control your computer — instead of clicking icons and folders, you type commands and press Enter. It looks intimidating at first because there's no menu telling you what to do, but it's actually simpler underneath: every command is just a short word or two, and the same handful of commands cover almost everything you'll need.

"Terminal" and "shell" get used almost interchangeably, but technically: the terminal is the window itself, and the shell is the program running inside it that actually reads your commands and runs them. The most common shell is called Bash, which is why people often say "the Bash prompt" — it's the default shell on Linux and Mac, and available on Windows too (through Git Bash, which this whole track assumes you have).

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think about what actually reads and runs your typed commands.
blocks.statement: The "shell" is the program that reads the commands you type and actually runs them, while the "terminal" is just the window it runs in.
blocks.explanation: The terminal is the window; the shell (like Bash) is the program inside it interpreting your commands.

blocks.body: Why bother, when clicking folders works fine? Because the terminal lets you do things a mouse can't: run a program with exact options, chain several steps together instantly, repeat the exact same action later without re-clicking through menus, and — most importantly for this track — every tool you'll use to actually ship a real project (Git, npm, Expo, deployment tools) is a command-line tool first. Some have a friendly app wrapped around them, but the terminal is the one interface all of them share.

highlights.text: every tool you'll use to actually ship a real project

blocks.body: You'll see a prompt — a short line ending in $ or > — waiting for you to type. After typing a command, press Enter to run it. If nothing seems to happen for a second, that's normal; some commands are just fast and quiet when they succeed. If something goes wrong, the terminal almost always prints an error message explaining what — reading that message is the single most useful debugging skill you can build.

code.caption: A typical prompt — the $ just means "waiting for your command", it is not something you type yourself.

blocks.question: What is the key practical reason this whole track uses the terminal instead of just apps with buttons?
options: Git, hosting, and app-building tools are all command-line tools at their core
Buttons are slower to render than text
Terminals use less battery than normal apps
blocks.explanation: Git, package managers, Expo, and deployment tools are fundamentally command-line tools — some have GUIs layered on top, but the terminal is the shared interface.

blocks.robotComment: pwd, ls, cd — three commands, and you can already explore your whole computer. 🗺️
blocks.body: Your files live in folders inside folders — this is called a directory tree, and the terminal always has you "standing" inside one folder at a time, called the current directory. Three commands let you find your way around it: pwd prints where you currently are, ls lists what's inside the current folder, and cd changes which folder you're standing in.

code.code:
$ pwd
/c/Users/maya

$ ls
Desktop  Documents  Downloads  Pictures
code.caption: pwd ("print working directory") shows where you are; ls ("list") shows what's there.

blocks.body: To move into a folder, use cd followed by its name — this is called changing directory. To go back up one level (into the folder that contains the one you're in), use cd .. — two dots mean "the parent folder". You can chain a full path in one go too, like cd Documents/projects, instead of moving one folder at a time.

code.caption: cd Documents moves in one level; cd .. moves back out one level.

blocks.sentence: The command ___ moves you back up one level, into the parent of the folder you are currently in.
blocks.explanation: Two dots (..) always mean "the parent folder" — cd .. steps up one level in the folder tree.

blocks.body: Typing out full folder names gets tedious fast, so the terminal has a shortcut: start typing a name and press Tab — it auto-completes as far as it can, and if there's more than one match, pressing Tab twice lists them. This is called tab completion, and using it constantly is one of the biggest speed differences between a beginner and someone comfortable at the command line.

Two more shortcuts worth knowing right away: cd by itself (no folder name) jumps straight back to your home folder from anywhere, and cd - jumps back to whichever folder you were in just before your last cd. Both save you from typing out a long path you'd otherwise have to retrace by hand.

blocks.question: Which command prints the full path of the folder you are currently standing in?
blocks.explanation: pwd ("print working directory") always tells you exactly where you currently are in the folder tree.

blocks.statement: Pressing Tab while typing a folder name will try to auto-complete it for you.
blocks.explanation: Tab completion fills in as much of the name as it can, saving you from typing long folder or file names out in full.

blocks.robotComment: mkdir makes folders, touch makes empty files — the two commands you'll use to start almost every project. 📁
blocks.body: Beyond navigating, you'll constantly need to create and clear away files and folders. mkdir ("make directory") creates a new folder. touch creates a new, empty file (its original purpose was updating a file's timestamp, but creating an empty file with it became the everyday habit). Both take the name of what you want to create as an argument — extra text typed right after the command.

code.code:
$ mkdir my-project
$ cd my-project
$ touch index.js
$ ls
index.js
code.caption: Creating a new folder, moving into it, then creating an empty file inside it.

blocks.body: To delete things, rm ("remove") deletes a file, and rm -r ("recursive") deletes a folder along with everything inside it. This is the one command in this whole lesson to treat with real caution: unlike deleting through your file explorer, the terminal has no recycle bin or trash — rm deletes immediately and permanently.

code.caption: rm deletes a single file; rm -r deletes a folder and everything inside it, permanently.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 This one's worth getting right before you ever run rm for real.
blocks.statement: Files deleted with rm in the terminal go to a recycle bin or trash folder, just like deleting them normally.
blocks.explanation: rm deletes immediately with no recycle bin — always double-check the name (and folder) before running it.

blocks.body: A few small letters after a command like this, written with a dash, are called flags (or options) — they change how the command behaves. -r on rm means "recursive: apply this to the folder and everything inside it". Most commands support several flags, and you can usually see them by adding --help after the command name, e.g. rm --help.

blocks.sentence: Running rm -r on a folder deletes it and everything inside it ___ — there is no recycle bin to recover it from.
blocks.explanation: The terminal has no undo for rm — it deletes right away, which is why the -r flag deserves extra caution.

blocks.question: What does the mkdir command do?
blocks.explanation: mkdir stands for "make directory" — directory is just another word for folder.

blocks.robotComment: Every real software project you will ever touch uses this. 🔧
blocks.body: Version control is a system that tracks every change made to a project's files over time, who made each change, and why. Instead of ending up with files named report-final.docx, report-final-v2.docx, and report-final-REALLY-final.docx, version control keeps one set of files with a complete, searchable history behind it — and Git is by far the most widely used version control system in the world.

In Git, a project tracked this way is called a repository (or "repo" for short) — just a folder that Git is watching. Each saved snapshot of the project is called a commit, and every commit has a short message describing what changed. Over time, this builds a full timeline you can look back through, compare, or even travel back to if something breaks.

blocks.statement: A Git "commit" is a saved snapshot of the project at a specific point in time, along with a message describing the change.
blocks.explanation: Each commit captures exactly what the project looked like at that moment, plus a short human-readable message about why.

blocks.body: Why does this matter so much? Three big reasons: you can always undo a mistake by going back to an earlier commit; you can see exactly what changed and when, which is invaluable when something breaks and you need to find out why; and it lets multiple people work on the same project at once without overwriting each other's work — which is the subject of the next level, GitHub.

highlights.text: multiple people work on the same project at once

blocks.question: What is a Git "repository"?
options: A folder that Git is tracking the history of
A single saved snapshot of a project
blocks.explanation: A repository (repo) is simply a project folder that Git watches and keeps a history for.

blocks.robotComment: init once, then add + commit over and over — that's basically the whole daily loop. 🔁
blocks.body: To start tracking a project, run git init inside its folder — this creates a hidden .git folder where Git will store the entire history. You only ever do this once per project. From then on, saving progress is a two-step habit: git add tells Git which changed files to include in the next snapshot, and git commit actually takes that snapshot.

code.code:
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /my-project/.git/
code.caption: Run once, inside your project folder, to start tracking it with Git.

blocks.body: git add takes a file name, or a . to mean "everything that changed". This moves those changes into what's called the staging area — a holding zone for exactly what will go into the next commit. Splitting it into two steps (add, then commit) lets you group related changes together and leave unrelated ones out, instead of every commit having to include absolutely everything you touched.

code.caption: Stage one specific file, or stage everything that changed with a single dot.

blocks.body: Once changes are staged, git commit -m "message" saves them as a permanent point in the project's history, with the text after -m as the description of what changed. Good commit messages are short and specific — "fix login button not responding" is far more useful later than "stuff" or "updates".

code.caption: The -m flag lets you write the commit message directly, right after the command.

blocks.sentence: The command ___ moves changed files into the staging area, ready to be committed.
blocks.explanation: git add stages changes; git commit then permanently saves whatever is currently staged.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think carefully about how often each of these actually runs.
blocks.statement: You need to run git init every single time you make a new commit.
blocks.explanation: git init runs only once, the very first time you start tracking a project — after that, it's just add and commit, repeated as often as you like.

blocks.question: What does the -m flag do on the git commit command?
options: Lets you write the commit message directly in the command
Moves a file to a new location
blocks.explanation: -m is short for "message" — it lets you attach the commit's description right in the same command.

blocks.robotComment: git status is the command you'll run more than any other — it's always safe, and always useful. 🔍
blocks.body: git status shows you the current state of your project: which files are changed but not yet staged, which are staged and ready to commit, and which aren't being tracked at all. Running it constantly — before add, before commit, whenever you're unsure — is one of the simplest habits that prevents most Git mistakes, since it never changes anything, only reports.

code.code:
$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   index.js
code.caption: git status reports what changed, without modifying anything — always safe to run.

blocks.body: git log shows the project's full commit history — each commit's unique ID, author, date, and message, newest first. This is how you actually use all that history you've been building: scrolling back to see what changed and when, or finding the exact commit to compare against or return to.

code.code:
$ git log
commit a1b2c3d...
Author: Maya
Date:   Tue Sep 1

    Add the login form
code.caption: git log lists commits from newest to oldest, each with its message.

blocks.statement: Running git status changes or commits any files.
blocks.explanation: git status is purely informational — it only reports the current state, it never modifies anything.

blocks.body: Not everything belongs in version control — things like dependency folders, build output, or files containing secrets (API keys, passwords) should never be committed. A .gitignore file, placed in the project's root folder, lists file and folder patterns that Git should simply ignore — it never even offers to stage them, no matter how many times you run git add ..

code.caption: A typical .gitignore: one pattern per line — here, a dependency folder, a secrets file, and any .log file.

blocks.sentence: A file named ___ lists file and folder patterns that Git should never track or stage.
blocks.explanation: .gitignore tells Git which files and folders to leave alone entirely — useful for secrets, build output, and dependency folders.

blocks.question: Why should a file containing API keys or passwords typically be listed in .gitignore?
options: Because committing it would permanently save it in the project's shared history
Because Git can't handle text files with symbols in them
Because it would make git status stop working
blocks.explanation: Once a secret is committed, it lives in the project history — .gitignore stops it from ever being staged or committed in the first place.
